posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
I'll be there too. I'm going to ask if I can have my Leia hologram in the display section. Also, Joy's been bugging me to write up something and so I have 4 or 5 ideas. Any comments or preferences?

"An overview of holographic aberrations"

Basically an overview of what aberrations in holography are, how they show up in an image and why they occur; can they be fixed? If so, how?

"A new colour map for diffractive processes"

Colour maps are basically based on the 1931 CIE chart (based on experiments done in 1929). However, the 1931 CIE was based on print colour and used fairly broadband primaries. The subjects (only about 20 of them, by the way, in the first run experiments - hardly a representative group!) were asked to match colours from three lamps which emitted broad band colour. Today we're used to seeing fairly narrow band sources from lasers and leds and so the reproduction of colour should be based on a colour map that reflects this narrow band illumination. In particular, I think holography may benefit, since I'm going to propose a scheme whereby the exposures/ratio of exposures of a colour hologram may be read off from the coordinates of the colour map. I gave a back-of-an-envelope presentation of this to Hiroshi (actually a back-of-a-napkin presentation at the OSA meeting in Miami ) and he asked about 4 colour primaries, so I extended my scheme to four, or any number, of colours. I think I've found that there is a reason why 4 or more colours are better than three.

"Overcoming cross talk in colour, laser transmission holograms"

Pretty self explanatory, I hope

"Dcg as a resist material 2"

A follow up on the paper at Holopak in 2008. At that time, I wanted to go through the entire process of making a dcg resist hologram, electro-forming it to make a shim and then copying the shim. I didn't have time for all of that, so maybe I may be able to do that this time.

Finally (and a little bit out on a limb): "Wavelet transforms as a possible method of real-time holography from digital imagery" You connect a medium to a computer, show up a 3d graphic and have it show up as a hologram in real time. This is, as you may imagine, a little *outre*, but I've been playing with this idea for the better part of a year and have had several people ask me write it up, so this may be a venue.

By the way, And Now for Something Completely Different, if anyone is in San Diego on October 5th, I'm giving an Osher lecture on 3D vision and holography ( [http://securelamp.csusm.edu/extstudies/ ... p?cid=1813](http://securelamp.csusm.edu/extstudies/el/rp/course_details.php?cid=1813) - the fourth one down). I believe anyone may be there and it's free.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
Kaveh

Sorry, I just get a little peeved when people in academia or in high corporate positions dismiss important technical points or valid objections to statements without a single thought, because I'm not in academia or in some exalted corporate position. I still can't seem to get "experts" to understand that Kogelnik is a scalar theory, not a vector one. Yet, I still hear that apparently there is a difference "in Kogelnik" between the efficiency of a hologram reconstructed in s or in p polarisaton. I've frequently asked people in high corporate and academic standing exactly where in the Kogelnik equations does one enter the vector state of the reconstruction and these very same people either scoff or turn away - in fact, anything but answer the question. Don't even get me started on the common fallacy that photons can interfere! As a graduate from Imperial in the Theoretical Physics Dept working on Quantum Gravity theories, I do know a little bit about the maths of optics but these high end corporate and academic types simply dismiss anyone they don't recognise. It seems a strange behaviour mode, when an academic should actually choose to further their knowledge, not use it as a cudgel!

Anyway, apologies again.

Jsfisher, thanks for the offer. I need to do a little bit of background before starting on the guts of the colour maps. I had to go to India for the last two weeks which threw everything off-kilter for me.

Bill, I do believe that a map would be useful. The present CIE chart is a little outdated and seems to refer to a colour scheme meant more for reflective or transmissive colour reproduction, not diffractive colour reproduction. I've read the papers of Kubota and Hans B, but they seem to be empirical with no underlying theoretical foundation. While empirical data is useful, my belief is that it doesn't lend itself to explore differing modelling systems. There seems to be an acceptance that 4 colours are better than 3 (and apparently 5 are better than 4), but no explanation as to why, no theoretical model based on cone sensitivity. The mammalian eye/brain system cannot perform Fourier Transforms (the ear actually can, which is why some people can pick out the harmonics in a musical note), so how does the retina "know" how many colours impinge upon it? While I was at the OSA meeting in Miami, I happened to get into conversation with Hiroshi who asked me about 4 colours. I thought about it a little and I think I may have a theoretical answer, but I need to "massage" the idea a little.

posts.content_md:
But Keveh, these proceedings will never be "out". They will always be "in" servers, requiring technology to view. Access can always and frivolously be denied. Nothing is being produced or "put out". 

Not ALL change is good. A real book isn't the same as data stored on a server. I thought I was creating something real, not an email message that can be modified or deleted with the push of a button, or lost because of a Norton created virus in Microsoft products or the electricity shuts off globally for a few months. Something real that won't require legacy software on antique equipment to view 20 years from now. Something that is proven to be survivable 50 years (or 400 years) into the future because of redundancy. Despite the best intentions of the organizers and their optimism and confidence in electronic data, and despite the incompetence of the China conference producers of their proceedings and the limited distribution of the Wales proceedings, I still feel ripped off.

posts.author: PinkysBrain
posts.content_md:
Slightly on topic :

With some of the print on demand services you can have restricted access to books, so there really is no excuse not to offer paper proceedings for those attending who want them and don't mind paying a little extra for the privilege.

As for the open access discussion ... from a science point of view it's of course optimal, but with conferences where most of the contributors are from industry rather than academia authors seem fine with the papers never being easily accessible and don't make any effort to make preprints available (whereas with something like Siggraph you can almost make a complete proceedings before the conference takes place). In some areas people seem only interested in acknowledgement within the small peer group able to attend their conferences, and holography seems definitely one of those areas.

Open access might be what I as an outsider want, but I don't think most of the people actually doing the work want it ... big thanks to Kaveh for spreading at least some of the information outside the inner circle regardless BTW.
